extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's The Rising Sea)
extracted.subtask_description: Reading and working through textbook material on Serre's criterion for normality, the 27 lines on a cubic surface, and cohomology & base change theorems; includes exercises, proofs, and examples used to verify algebraic-geometry statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's criterion for normality (R1 + S2)
rubrics_metrics.description: R1 + S2 implies normal: for a Noetherian ring A (stalk-local statement) if A satisfies R1 and S2 then A is integrally closed (normal). In particular, for a Noetherian local ring (A, m) of dimension d satisfying R1 and S2 one gets that A is an integrally closed integral domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy given: reduce to the integral domain case, show integrally closed in total fraction ring, use induction on dimension for the general case. Notes: A satisfies R0 and S1 (so reduced) by Exercise 26.3.B; the integral-domain case is treated first as easier and motivating. See exercises 26.3.F, 26.3.G and the use of Hartogs’s lemma and localizations at codimension 1 primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: S2 (depth) condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Property S2: for a Noetherian local ring (A, m) of dimension > 1, S2 requires depth(A) ≥ 2 (equivalently depth of A/(x) > 0 for nonzero x in m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To verify S2 for a normal ring A: pick nonzero x ∈ m, show depth A/(x) > 0. The textbook shows a contradiction if depth=0 by producing y with ym = 0 in A/(x) and using integrality arguments in the fraction field and Hartogs’s Lemma to contradict. The argument uses that normal ⇒ integral domain and integrally closed localizations at codimension 1 primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: R1 condition (regular in codimension 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Property R1: A is regular in codimension 1; equivalently for every prime p of codimension 1, the localization Ap is regular (hence integrally closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Serre's criterion: R1 ensures Api is integrally closed for codimension 1 primes, which is used to show integrality statements about elements integral over A. See Theorem 12.5.8 equivalences referenced in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normality is a stalk-local condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Normality can be checked stalk-locally: to prove A normal it suffices to check the condition on local rings (or equivalently at localizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to reduce Serre's criterion to the Noetherian local ring case: prove (†) for (A,m) local and then conclude globally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral closure criterion (element test)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A is integrally closed in its fraction ring: show that any x ∈ K(A) integral over A already lies in A. Concretely, write x = f/g with f,g ∈ A (g a non-zerodivisor) and show f ∈ (g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text proves this by induction on dimension: localize at primes not containing a chosen non-zerodivisor t to reduce codimension and use the inductive hypothesis; then use that t is a non-zerodivisor on A/(g) so localization map is injective, concluding f is zero in A/(g). Exercises 26.3.G and 5.5.7 are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrally closed in total fraction ring ⇒ product of integral domains (Lemma 26.3.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is reduced with finitely many minimal primes p1,...,pn and R is integrally closed in its total fraction ring, then R is a finite product of integrally closed integral domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the natural map R → ∏ Rpi, identification of the total fraction ring with ∏ Rpi, and the fact that idempotents of the total fraction ring lie in R because R is integrally closed. Exercises 26.3.H and 26.3.I continue the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Hartogs’s Lemma to extend functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic Hartogs’s Lemma (11.3.11) is used to show elements defined off a codimension ≥2 subset extend to all of Spec A when A is integrally closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the S2 argument and in extending morphisms from punctured neighbourhoods (later, in 27.4), Hartogs’s Lemma is used to deduce global vanishing or extension from local information at codimension 1 points. The lemma relies on integral-closedness hypotheses of localizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and dimension properties of incidence correspondences (Y and Z)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct incidence correspondences parametrizing (singular point p on cubic X) and (line ℓ in cubic X): Y ⊂ P19 × P3 is a P15-bundle over P3 and Z ⊂ P19 × G(1,3) is a P15-bundle over G(1,3); these are irreducible smooth varieties of dimensions 18 and 19 respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: build Y and Z as explicit projective bundles to control dimensions; use these to show the locus of singular cubics (Δ) is irreducible codimension 1 and to analyze lines on cubics. Exercises 27.2.D and 27.3.A walk through these constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension/upper-semicontinuity arguments for generic finiteness of fibers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dimension counts and upper semicontinuity of fibre dimension to deduce that for a projective morphism π: Z → P19 (lines in cubics), the generic fibre has finite (positive finite) cardinality: 'most cubic surfaces have a finite number of lines'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply existence of an example with finitely many lines (Fermat cubic) and upper semicontinuity (Exercise 11.4.A / Theorem 11.4.1) to deduce surjectivity of π and generic finiteness; see Exercise 27.3.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: No first-order deformations of a line on a smooth cubic (Theorem 27.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ℓ is a line in a regular (smooth) cubic surface X then [ℓ] is an isolated reduced point of the fibre π−1([X]) (i.e., the line has no first-order deformations in X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses local coordinates: parametrize nearby lines by (a,a',b,b') and substitute into f to obtain four equations; work modulo (a,a',b,b')^2 to force linear terms to vanish using regularity along ℓ (quadratics Cx(t), Cy(t) have no common roots). This yields multiplicity one for each line in the fibre; see Exercises 27.3.C–27.3.E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite flatness and degree-constancy of π over smooth locus
rubrics_metrics.description: Over P19 \ Δ (the smooth cubic locus), the projection π: Z → P19 is finite and flat (indeed finite étale when base field is algebraically closed), and hence the number of lines (counted correctly) is constant on each connected component; for cubics this degree is 27.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine Theorem 27.3.1 (reduced isolated points) with π projective and Z regular (Cohen–Macaulay) to apply Miracle Flatness (26.2.11) and Theorem 18.1.8; use Fermat cubic to compute the degree=27. See the proof of Theorem 27.1.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariance of the configuration of lines via finite étale coverings
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a finite étale cover W → P19 \ Δ parametrizing a cubic surface together with an ordered list of its 27 distinct lines; connectedness and lifting along this cover allow identification of the intersection configuration of lines on any two smooth cubics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct W as the open-and-closed locus in the 27th fibered power of Z where the 27 lines are distinct (Exercise 27.3.F). Use connected components and lifting to compare labelled lines between surfaces and deduce combinatorial intersection data is constant; this underlies the later identification of symmetry group W(E6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicontinuity Theorem for cohomology (28.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is proper with Y Noetherian and F a coherent sheaf on X flat over Y, then q ↦ dimκ(q) Hp(Xq, F|Xq) is an upper semicontinuous function on Y for each p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: ranks of cohomology groups on fibres are upper semicontinuous in proper flat families. Used to deduce existence of dense open where Rpπ_*F is locally free. See reference to proof in §28.2. Examples show dimensions may jump in families (e.g., line bundles on an elliptic curve).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grauert's theorem (vector-bundle and base-change criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is proper with Y reduced and locally Noetherian, F coherent on X flat over Y, and q ↦ hp(Xq,F|Xq) is locally constant on Y, then Rpπ_*F is locally free and φ_p^Z (base-change map) is an isomorphism for all ψ: Z → Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No Noetherian hypothesis on Y beyond locally Noetherian is needed; consequence: locally constant fibre dimensions on a reduced base allow gluing into a vector bundle and identify fibres with cohomology of fibres. See Theorem 28.1.5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology and Base Change theorem (28.1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π proper, Y locally Noetherian, F coherent and flat over Y, and the base-change map φ_p^q is surjective at a point q. Then (i) there is a neighborhood U of q such that for any ψ: Z → U the base-change map φ_p^Z is an isomorphism; (ii) φ_{p-1}^q is an isomorphism. Equivalently, surjectivity at q ⇔ (Rpπ_*F)_q is free (Rpπ_*F locally free near q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relates surjectivity of the natural map on fibres to local freeness and nearby base-change isomorphisms. The proof uses the local criterion for flatness; consequences include that constancy of hp in a neighborhood follows from these hypotheses. See Theorem 28.1.6 and Exercises 28.1.B–C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat base change for cohomology (special case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohomology commutes with flat base change: if ψ is flat then the natural base-change morphism φ_p^Z is an isomorphism (Theorem 24.2.8 referenced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an easy case where base-change holds. Combined with Grauert and Cohomology-and-Base-Change to handle more general situations when flatness of ψ or flatness/local-freeness of Rpπ_*F is available.
